title: Straw dogs
hookLine: heaven and earth aren't sentimental; they treat things like straw dogs used in a ritual (Tao Te Ching 5)

cards: Does the rain know it's your wedding day? Months of planning. The chairs are out on the lawn, flowers tied to the ends of the rows, and at ten in the morning the sky opens.
It's very hard not to take it personally. Why today? Why us?
But the same rain falls on the farmer who prayed for it, on the parking lot, on the stray cat under the porch. It isn't aimed.
Chapter five of the Tao Te Ching says something blunt about this, with a strange object: a dog made of straw.

teach.b: First, heaven and earth aren't sentimental. They don't act out of a wish to be kind, the chapter says; in Legge's words, "they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with."
And the sage treats people the same way. That can sound cold. Hold on to it a moment.
Second, what a straw dog was. Another old Chinese book, the Zhuangzi, home of the river god who met the sea on day one thousand thirteen, describes them.
Before the ritual, straw dogs were kept in fine boxes, wrapped in embroidered cloth, handled with care by people who had fasted.
After the offering, they were thrown out, walked over in the road, swept up by grass-gatherers to burn.
Honored, then discarded. Not out of spite. The ritual was simply over.

Third, a bellows. The space between heaven and earth, the chapter goes on, is like a bellows: empty, yet never used up, and the more it moves, the more comes out. The world isn't keeping score of anyone.
It just keeps breathing. And a quiet warning: lots of talk wears out fast; better to keep to the center. Fourth, a neighbor with another spirit.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says God "sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." There, rain on everyone is a sign of the Father's goodness, and a reason to love even enemies.
In chapter five, the same impartial rain shows that heaven isn't sentimental.
Two traditions, two meanings, the same weather.

how: Readers of chapter five sometimes use the straw dogs as a reminder that misfortune isn't aimed at them, letting events be what they are before deciding how to respond.

games.q: it rains on the outdoor wedding you planned for months. how does chapter five see the rain?
o: the sky has something against you.
it isn't personal: the rain falls on everything alike.
it must be a punishment for something.
games.why: heaven and earth aren't sentimental, chapter five says; they deal with all things alike, like straw dogs. the rain isn't aimed.

practice: Think of something recent that wasn't aimed at you: a delayed flight, a cold that came the week of a trip, a price that went up.
Notice the why-me story your mind has wrapped around it, and set the story down beside the event, so you're looking at the event alone.
If you pray, you can hold it in prayer just as it is; if not, breathe out and let it be weather.
